A.summary: Evil is an existence and not a privation, because evil admits of degrees while privation does not.

B.summary: Evil is a privation that admits of degrees based on distance from the good, and evil depends on good.

c1.text: Privation does not admit of more or less.

c2.text: 'This is lacking' and 'this is not lacking' are contradictory, allowing no middle ground.

c3.text: Existence admits of more or less, since there can be degrees of perfection in existence.

c4.text: Evil admits of degrees (some evil things are more evil than others).

c8.text: Concepts involving privation (such as inequality or dissimilarity) admit of more or less depending on distance from perfection/good.

c9.text: Something more lacking in goodness is more evil.

c10.text: Privation does not exist in itself, but increases or decreases according to the cause producing it.

c11.text: Good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good.

c12.text: Evil can exist independently of good.

c13.text: Evil is a privation that admits of degrees.

a.note: B argues evil is a privation (c6), whereas A concludes evil is not a privation (c5, contrary of c6).

b.note: Both A and B take the degree of evil (c4) as an established premise.

c.note: B derives that good can exist without evil but not vice versa (c11), whereas A views evil as an independent existence (c12).
